name: dosbox-x
desc: DOSBox with accurate emulation and wide testing
why: Accurate DOS emulation is a window into old hardware and software, though DOSBox is a known name.

brief.what_it_is: DOSBox-X is an open-source, cross-platform DOS emulator for running DOS games and applications on modern Windows, Linux, and macOS, and as a DOS program itself. It emulates a PC of the IBM PC/XT/AT class, and also NEC PC-98, AX, and DOS/V systems. The README says it also runs Windows 1.0 through Windows ME as guest systems, with Windows 3.x and 9x officially supported. It is a fork of DOSBox, taken from DOSBox SVN Daum in mid-2011, and it is a separate project now.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says the original DOSBox focuses on DOS games and uses game-oriented kludges, while he wanted changes that real DOS systems and non-game software need. The stated goal is accurate enough emulation to support historical preservation, testing, and new DOS development, covering pre-2000 DOS and Windows 9x hardware.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes the program as a set of incremental changes on top of the DOSBox codebase, with many options to tweak the virtual machine, from an original IBM PC up to late-1990s configurations. Behaviour is set through a .conf file and command-line options, and a GUI drop-down menu and built-in configuration tool are included. Emulation covers CPUs up to Pentium III and MMX, IDE and disk controllers, 3dfx Voodoo and Glide, NE2000 networking, and FluidSynth and MT-32 MIDI.

commands_seen.context: Command-line option that disables commands which could reach the host system; the README recommends it if security matters.
Config setting that turns off FPU emulation so QBasic or Turbo Basic runtimes use software floating point, which the README says fixes certain file-size comparisons in some games.
Config option; on Windows it tries to match the physical keyboard layout. Other platforms default to a US keyboard.

brief.install_notes: Windows has a 32/64-bit setup installer (Win7+ recommended, XP+ also supported) and 32-bit portable packages (9x/NT4+). Linux is available as a Flatpak on Flathub or an RPM on Fedora Copr, with Raspberry Pi also supported. macOS has separate Intel and ARM builds; the SDL2 build needs macOS 12 or later. A DOS version (HX-DOS package) can run on a real DOS system, but not every feature works there. Source is available as zip or tar.gz, with build steps in BUILD.md and install steps in INSTALL.md. Config is via a .conf file, and language files go in a languages directory.
brief.standout: Its scope is unusual: it aims to cover essentially every pre-2001 PC hardware scenario, including PC-98 and DOS/V, and to run Windows 9x guests, which the README describes as its main departure from DOSBox. The README also states its limits openly, saying it will not emulate Pentium 4 or later, post-2001 hardware, or Windows Vista and later, and it points users to Bochs, QEMU, 86Box, or PCem for those.
brief.status: Maintained, based on the homepage. It lists a latest release of 2026.10.01 dated October 1, 2026, and the README describes a monthly release pattern with new versions at the start of each month, plus development builds. I could not check the current date or the commit history, so the most recent activity is taken from the homepage's claim. The README says the main developer has limited time and asks for help.
brief.caveats: The README says it is not secure: it is not a containment tool, so do not run it as root or Administrator, and do not use it on a secure system. The Windows-only features include Direct3D output and automatic drive mounting. Full FPU precision is not emulated, which can break some software. Cycle-accurate timing is not a goal. The README also contains a legal notice: users in jurisdictions that enforce OS-level age verification may only use the main-osfree branch, and are barred from the master branch. The macOS SDL2 build needs macOS 12 or later. I did not check the license beyond the README, which says GPL v2.
quotes: DOSBox-X is a cross-platform DOS emulator based on the DOSBox project (www.dosbox.com).

Our goal is to eventually make DOSBox-X a complete emulation package that covers all pre-2000 DOS and Windows 9x based system scenarios, including peripherals, motherboards, CPUs, and all manner of hardware that was made for PC hardware of that time.
DOSBox-X cannot claim to be a "secure" application.
